topic.title: Too expensive to keep
topic.claim: When a brand-new manager suddenly has strong opinions about your salary, the problem was never your performance.
topic.behaviour: Managers quietly pressure expensive employees to resign right before appraisal cycles, citing vague 'budget' instead of performance.
topic.mechanism: A resignation leaves no severance, no paper trail and a clean budget line. Firing someone for being well-paid looks bad on record; a voluntary exit doesn't.
topic.group: Salaried employees, 24-32, mid-career, approaching their first big appraisal
topic.moment: A manager you've known for eight weeks calls you in right before appraisal season and says nothing you did was wrong, just that the budget doesn't support your role.

turn.believed: The company has a genuine budget problem and you drew the short straw.
turn.actually: You're being quietly priced out before your raise is due, dressed up as a budget conversation.

topic.because: A resignation costs the company nothing and shows up nowhere. Firing someone for earning well looks bad; asking them to leave on their own doesn't.
topic.payoff: If a manager you've met twice suddenly has an opinion about your pay, check the calendar before you check your performance.
topic.send_to: Anyone whose new manager just got weirdly specific about 'team budget.'
real_details: New manager appointed roughly two months before the conversation
Timed right before an October appraisal cycle
topic.news_peg: Bengaluru employee's viral account of manager pressure ahead of the Oct 24 appraisal cycle (2026-10-22)
topic.why_now: Appraisal season is live right now and this exact story just went viral

score.why: Office politics everyone's lived near, with a clean test: a new manager's sudden opinion about your pay is a clock, not a review.

violations: Hard failure 12: a hidden motive and deliberate plan stated as fact, with no allowance for a real budget problem. Lines: "Nobody asked you to leave. They asked you to want to."; "A resignation looks like your choice. No severance talk, no awkward record, and the budget line comes out clean."; the cover and slide 1 claim "it was never about your work." The only source is one unverified viral account, and the legal source says pressured resignations can count as constructive dismissal. So 'no awkward record' is not safe to state flatly.
notes: Slide 4: Drop the certainty that someone planned it. 'Nobody asked you to leave. They asked you to want to.' reads as a proven intent. Reframe as what the setup rewards, not what the manager schemed. For example: whether or not anyone meant it, this kind of chat ends well for the company only if you walk. Show it through the effect, not a claimed plan.

Slide 5: The mechanism is over-asserted. 'No severance talk, no awkward record, budget line comes out clean' is stated as guaranteed fact. Keep the core because: firing someone with good feedback for earning well looks bad, while a resignation looks like the person's own choice. Cut the 'no record' and 'clean budget line' claims, or soften them into what the company gets out of it. Also remove the stock opener 'Here's the part that makes it work.'

Slide 4 and slide 5: These overlap. Both say 'it looks like your choice'. Say it once. Use the freed space for one new beat: the reader's own reaction afterwards (you start updating the CV and feel it was your idea), which makes the turn land emotionally and lifts eq.

Cover and slide 1: 'isn't discussing your work' and 'it was never about your work' are absolute. Make the claim sharper but defensible: the timing says more than the feedback does, or a budget talk this close to appraisal is about your pay, not your work. The slide 6 test already supports that wording.

Slide 6: 'Your work didn't change in those eight weeks. The date on that invite did.' is a good line. The bold closer then restates the cover's point. End on the sharper image, the date on the invite, and trim the closing instruction so it stays a test and does not read as advice.

sources.fact: A Bengaluru employee alleged in a social-media post that a manager who had been in the role about two months asked him to resign before the next appraisal cycle, saying his pay was too high for the team's budget. The claim is unverified, and the company has not responded.
sources.excerpt: asking him to submit his resignation before the next appraisal cycle. | his salary was too high for the team's budget. | [Page notes, paraphrased by the fetch tool: the manager changed about two months earlier; the salary revision was expected around 24 October; the employee knew of no performance problems; the claims come from his social-media post and have not been independently verified; there is no company response.]

sources.fact: In X v. Registrar, MP High Court (Feb 2022), the Supreme Court held that a resignation given amid an unfair work environment was not voluntary and amounted to constructive dismissal. This is legal context and does not show that managers pressure expensive employees to resign before appraisals.

cover.headline: A budget chat before appraisal is about your [pay], not your work
cover.sub: Especially from a manager you met eight weeks ago.

paragraphs:
A budget chat before appraisal is about your pay, not your work. Especially from a manager you met eight weeks ago.
Swipe to read →
slides.why_swipe: What does that chat actually look like?

paragraphs: Your new manager joined two months ago. So far you've had one intro call and one team lunch where everyone shared their hobbies.
Then, a week before appraisals, an invite lands on your calendar. No agenda. Just "Quick chat?"
slides.why_swipe: What does the quick chat turn out to be?

paragraphs: They start kindly. Your work has been good. Nothing you did was wrong.
But the team budget doesn't really support your role at your level. You walk out thinking the company is in a tight spot, and you just drew the short straw.
slides.why_swipe: Is it really just bad luck?

paragraphs: Later you notice what the chat left out. No warning mail, no list of misses, no improvement plan. Only a soft line at the door: "Think about what's best for you."
**Whether anyone planned it or not, that chat only ends well for the company if you walk.**
slides.why_swipe: Why would walking suit them better than any other ending?

paragraphs: Maybe the budget really is tight. But letting go of someone with good feedback because they earn well looks bad. A resignation looks like your choice.
So that night you open Naukri and fix your CV. By Sunday it feels like your own idea.
slides.why_swipe: So what should you look at before you decide?

paragraphs: If a manager you've met twice suddenly has a view on your pay, check the calendar before you check your performance.
**Your work didn't change in those eight weeks. The date on that invite did.**

end.save: Come back to this the next time a new boss books a "quick chat" before appraisals.
end.send: Send it to the friend whose new manager just got weirdly specific about "team budget."

draft.caption: Has a new manager ever brought up "budget" a week before your appraisal? What exact line did they use on you?
draft.alt_text: A six-slide text carousel. The cover reads: A budget chat before appraisal is about your pay, not your work, especially from a manager you met eight weeks ago. The slides describe a manager who joined two months ago calling you in a week before appraisals, saying your work is fine but the team budget can't support your role, and suggesting you think about what's best for you. The post notes that, planned or not, such a chat only ends well for the company if you resign, since a resignation looks like your own choice, and that you end up updating your CV feeling it was your idea. It ends: your work didn't change in those eight weeks, the date on that invite did.
